street_smart.title: You get a message from an unknown number claiming they have compromising photos or videos of you, threatening to send them to your contacts unless you pay immediately — and warning you not to tell anyone or go to the police. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real incident: a Bengaluru woman died by suicide after alleging blackmail and harassment (NDTV, ThePrint). This scenario focuses on how to safely respond to an online blackmail threat — the mechanism scammers use — rather than the tragedy itself, since sextortion-style blackmail is a fast-growing and dangerous scam pattern. Not covered as a street-smart scenario in the last three weeks.
street_smart.situation: The message gives you a short deadline, demands payment to a UPI ID or wallet, and threatens to escalate if you involve police or tell family.

choices.text: Don't pay or reply. Block the sender on all platforms, screenshot everything as evidence first, report immediately to the National Cyber Crime helpline (1930) or cybercrime.gov.in, and tell a trusted family member or friend right away.
choices.feedback: Correct — paying or engaging never ends a blackmail attempt, it only confirms you're a paying target. Reporting fast to 1930 lets police request an emergency takedown before content spreads, and telling someone you trust removes the isolation the blackmailer is counting on to keep you silent.

choices.text: Pay the amount quietly to make it go away and never mention it to anyone.
choices.feedback: This is the trap — paying proves you'll pay, and blackmailers almost always return with bigger demands once they know it works on you. The secrecy they demand is the actual weapon here: isolation is what lets them keep control, not the content itself.

choices.text: Argue back and threaten to go to the police yourself, engaging directly with the blackmailer.
choices.feedback: Engaging can provoke an anxious or vindictive blackmailer into leaking out of spite or escalating threats for leverage. It's safer to go quiet toward them while you gather evidence and alert the real authorities in the background.

choices.text: Delete the messages and the contact immediately to erase all trace of it, then wait and see if anything happens.
choices.feedback: Deleting removes the evidence police need to trace the account and act — and content already sent may exist elsewhere regardless of what you delete. Ignoring it doesn't make the threat go away; reporting with evidence intact gives you real recourse.

takeaways: National Cyber Crime Helpline: 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in — available 24/7 and can request emergency takedown of leaked content within hours if you report fast.
Never pay a blackmailer — payment doesn't end the threat, it invites repeat demands.

You're not alone and you're not at fault — tell a trusted person immediately. Isolation is the blackmailer's main tool; confidential support is also available through helplines like iCall (9152987821).
